steps.title: Prepare SD‑RLU medium
steps.instruction: Make 500 mL of SD‑RLU: dissolve 3.35 g yeast nitrogen base (6.7 g/L) and 0.5 g amino‑acid mixture (1 g/L) together with 0.08 g L‑Histidine and 0.08 g L‑Tryptophan (each 0.16 g/L) in 450 mL deionized water, adjust pH to 6.5 if needed, autoclave, cool to ~55 °C and add 50 mL of 20 % glucose solution to obtain 2 % final glucose. For plates, add STAR agar L‑grade (2 % final) before autoclaving.

steps.title: Prepare YPD medium
steps.instruction: Make 500 mL of YPD: dissolve 5 g Bacto yeast extract (10 g/L), 10 g Bacto peptone (20 g/L) and 0.015 g adenine (0.03 g/L) in 450 mL deionized water, autoclave, cool to ~55 °C and add 50 mL of 20 % glucose solution to reach 2 % glucose. For plates, add STAR agar L‑grade (2 % final) before autoclaving.

steps.title: Prepare YPA medium
steps.instruction: Make 500 mL of YPA: dissolve 5 g Bacto yeast extract, 10 g Bacto peptone and 0.015 g adenine in 450 mL deionized water, autoclave, cool to ~55 °C and add 50 mL of 20 % potassium acetate solution to obtain 2 % potassium acetate final concentration.

steps.title: Prepare sporulation medium
steps.instruction: Make 500 mL of sporulation medium by dissolving ingredients (including 20 % potassium acetate) in 450 mL deionized water and autoclaving; the final medium contains 2 % potassium acetate.

steps.title: Prepare 2 mM β‑Estradiol stock
steps.instruction: Dissolve β‑Estradiol in 100 % ethanol to a 2 mM concentration, aliquot into 1.5 mL tubes and store at –30 °C.

steps.title: Yeast culture and sporulation induction
steps.instruction: a. Streak frozen yeast strains on YPD plates, then restreak single colonies onto SD‑RLU agar and incubate 30 °C for 2–3 days. b. Inoculate one colony into 3 mL SD‑RLU liquid, grow 24 h at 30 °C, 200 rpm. c. Dilute 800 µL of the overnight culture into 15 mL YPA in a 250 mL Erlenmeyer flask, incubate 16 h at 30 °C. d. Transfer the culture to a 50 mL conical tube, pellet at 2,150 × g for 3 min at RT, discard supernatant, rinse flask with 15 mL sterile water, combine rinse with pellet and repeat centrifugation. e. Resuspend the final pellet in sporulation medium to OD₆₀₀ = 2.0, transfer to a 250 mL flask and continue shaking. f. After 6 h, add β‑Estradiol stock to achieve a final concentration of 2 µM (add 2 mM stock accordingly) to induce NDT80 expression.

steps.title: Prepare microscopy samples
steps.instruction: a. At each desired time point, collect 200–300 µL of sporulating culture. b. Spin briefly at 500 × g for 10 s to form a soft pellet. c. Gently resuspend the pellet by pipetting at the tube bottom. d. Pipette ~5 µL of the concentrated suspension onto a 24 × 50 mm coverslip. e. Place an 18 × 18 mm coverslip on top to create a sandwich, spreading cells into a monolayer. f. Lightly press a Kimwipe on the top coverslip to absorb excess liquid. Proceed immediately to imaging.

steps.title: Acquire Z‑stack images
steps.instruction: Place the coverslip sandwich on a microscope slide and acquire 3D Z‑stacks using a Leica THUNDER Imager with a HC PL APO 100×/1.40 OIL objective; collect 40–50 slices at 0.21 µm intervals, capturing mCherry‑Spo20 51–91 fluorescence.

steps.title: Preprocess raw Z‑stack images
steps.instruction: a. Apply an image‑restoration or deconvolution method (e.g., Small Volume Computational Clearing in Leica software or equivalent) to reduce haze. b. Generate a 2D maximum‑intensity projection (MIP) from each cleared stack and export the MIP as a TIF file.

steps.title: Install and train custom CellPose model
steps.instruction: a. Install CellPose with its GUI following the official instructions (https://cellpose.readthedocs.io). b. Launch the GUI, import a representative subset of 2D MIP images, and manually trace boundaries of complete, alive cells only. c. Train a custom CellPose model using a learning rate of 0.1, weight decay of 0.0001, and 10,000 epochs; export the trained model file for later use.

steps.title: Segment cells and crop single‑cell images
steps.instruction: a. Apply the trained CellPose model to the full set of MIP images to segment all valid cells. b. For each segmented cell, crop a 200 × 200 px region centered on its centroid, producing three files per cell: (i) crop_image (raw crop), (ii) extract_image (crop with neighboring cells masked out), and (iii) gray_image (grayscale version of extract_image).

steps.title: Manually annotate prospore membranes
steps.instruction: a. In Fiji/ImageJ, create a stack image from all extract_image files (Image > Stacks > Images to Stack, check “Use title as labels”, Method = Copy (center)). b. Sort the stack by label (Image > Stacks > Tools > Stack Sorter, “Sort by Label”). c. For each slice, use the Freehand selection tool to trace each PSM, add the ROI to the ROI Manager, and repeat for all PSMs in the image. d. Save the ROI set as a .zip file (e.g., Stack.zip) in a dedicated folder; optionally also save the original stack as Stack.tif for quality control. (Optional: use an iPad with Apple Pencil via Spacedesk for drawing.)

steps.title: Convert ROIs to masks and build COCO dataset
steps.instruction: a. Ensure a sufficient number of ROIs (≈7,000 in the original study). b. Run the provided rois2mask.py script on each .zip file to generate binary mask images (pixel = 1 for ROI, 0 for background). c. Randomly split the image‑mask pairs into training, validation, and test sets using an 8:1:1 ratio, keeping each image paired with its mask. d. Execute create_coco_annotations.py to compile all pairs into a COCO‑format JSON annotation file required by MMdetection.

steps.title: Train DeMemSeg model
steps.instruction: a. Build the Docker image using the supplied Dockerfile (docker build -t dememseg-env:latest .). b. Inside the container, edit the configuration file (e.g., configs/dememseg_config.py) to set data_root and annotation‑file paths to the COCO dataset; optionally adjust hyper‑parameters. The final model used a ResNet‑50 backbone, SGD optimizer, learning rate 0.0025, batch size 4. c. Launch training from the container command line, monitor segm_mAP on the validation set (via log files or TensorBoard), and after completion select the checkpoint (.pth) with the highest performance (e.g., highest segm_mAP or segm_mAP_75).

steps.title: Set up inference Docker environment
steps.instruction: a. Clone the DeMemSeg repository (git clone https://github.com/MolCellBiol-tsukuba/DeMemSeg.git; cd DeMemSeg). b. Build the Docker image (docker build -t dememseg-env:latest .) and run a container with GPU access, mounting the current directory and exposing port 8888 (docker run -it --name dememseg_container --gpus all -v "$(pwd)":/workspace -p 8888:8888 dememseg-env:latest). c. Connect to the running container using VS Code with the Docker extension for convenient file editing and command execution.

steps.title: Run inference notebook on MIP images
steps.instruction: a. Copy your 2D MIP TIF files into a folder such as input_images/ inside the repository. b. Open the Jupyter notebook main_DeMemSeg.ipynb. c. Edit the initial cells to set the correct input‑image path and desired output‑folder path. d. Execute all notebook cells; the pipeline will (i) crop single cells using the custom CellPose model, (ii) segment PSMs with the pretrained DeMemSeg model, and (iii) optionally perform morphological analysis and generate plots.

steps.title: Locate and review output files
steps.instruction: a. After notebook completion, inspect the specified output directory for segmented mask images, JSON files containing instance coordinates, any generated figures, and CSV files. b. Verify that the results resemble expected segmentation quality; note that the pretrained model is optimized for images similar to those described in section A2 and performance may vary on very different data.

steps.title: Extract morphological features to CSV
steps.instruction: a. Run the provided script mmdetection_psm.py (available at https://github.com/MolCellBiol-tsukuba/DeMemSeg-train/blob/main/script/mmdetection_psm.py) to read the JSON output, decode RLE masks, and compute for each membrane: area, perimeter, major‑axis length, aspect ratio, roundness, compactness, seven Hu moments, Fourier descriptors, centroid (x, y) coordinates, and mean pixel intensity. b. The script aggregates all measurements into a single CSV file with one row per PSM, ready for downstream statistical analysis.

description: Validation of protocol This protocol and its core components have been used and validated in the following research article: Taguchi et al. [7]. Deep learning-based segmentation of 2D projection-derived overlapping prospore membrane in yeast. Cell Struct Funct . The robustness and reliability of this protocol are demonstrated by several key findings presented in the research article. Following systematic optimization, the final DeMemSeg model achieved strong quantitative performance metrics, including a segm_mAP of 0.670 and a segm_mAP_75 of 0.786, with visual validation confirming high individual IoU scores for representative instances (Figure 3 in [7]). Furthermore, the protocol's output was directly compared against the gold standard of manual expert annotation. This comparison revealed no statistically significant differences between morphological measurements (PSM length and roundness) derived from DeMemSeg’s automated segmentation and those from manual annotation for both WT and gip1 ∆ mutant cells (Figure 5B in [7]). Finally, the protocol's practical utility and generalization capabilities were confirmed by its successful application to two types of unseen data: dynamic time-lapse image sequences (Figure 4 in [7]) and the morphologically distinct gip1 ∆ mutant, which was not part of the training data. The ability to quantitatively distinguish the mutant phenotype from the WT population ( Figure 5 ) confirms that the protocol produces reliable and biologically meaningful results.
